# How To Stay Organized - Life

- **Source URL**: [https://life.berkeley.edu/how-to-stay-organized/](https://life.berkeley.edu/how-to-stay-organized/)
- **Crawled At**: 2026-07-16T08:44:31.609Z

## Content

![decorative image](https://life.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Milana_Cafe_EDITED.jpg) 

   By [Nina Takahashi](https://life.berkeley.edu/author/nina-takahashi/) 
 [[Home Berkeley - Life|Copy Link]][[Home Berkeley - Life|Email]][[Home Berkeley - Life|Print]][[Home Berkeley - Life|LinkedIn]]     7 MINUTE READ  Post Views: 61  
  [Study Tips](https://life.berkeley.edu/tag/study-tips/)    
## Organization 101
 
When I arrived at UC Berkeley as a first-year, I was burnt out. My high school schedule had been jam-packed — consisting of early morning dance practices, late night theater rehearsals, and a dozen student government meetings studded in between — so I’d resolved to keep my college schedule light. This resolve lasted all but one week. By the time I’d memorized the names of my professors, I’d already started working two part-time jobs, hosting game nights in my dorm room, and applying to clubs.
 
My story isn’t unique. Almost all of my friends are juggling two to twenty activities alongside academics; I’ve learned that it comes with the territory of being a Berkeley student. So, if you’re doing it all, how do you keep track of it all? This article compiles organizational tips and anecdotes from students to help you live your best Berkeley life.
 
### Berkeley Google Calendar, AKA bCal
 
At UC Berkeley, Google Calendar is king. You’ll be hard-pressed to find a student who doesn’t use the platform because the university itself uses it as part of our [bConnected communications](https://bconnected.berkeley.edu/services/welcome-uc-berkeley) ecosystem. The Google Calendar associated with your @berkeley.edu email is called bCal. By default, bCal usually sends a notification 10 to 30 minutes prior to an event, but you can customize the time and frequency of your notifications.
 
As with any other Google Calendar, you can [sync](https://support.google.com/calendar/answer/151674?hl=en&co=GENIE.Platform%3DiOS) your bCal to your iPhone or Android phone’s calendar. You can also [share](https://support.google.com/calendar/answer/37082?hl=en) your bCal with other people, and you can have multiple Google Calendars open at the same time, which helps with scheduling meetings.
 
“I live by my bCal schedule! I use this to track all classes, club meetings, and schedule-related things. I also put large school events (like midterms, finals, and paper due dates) on here, but not smaller homework tasks. I like to color-code my bCal based on class/work/personal to keep things visually neat!” — Shae, Class of 2029, majoring in English
 ![decorative image](https://life.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Shae_s-Google-Calendar_EDITED.jpg)
Shae’s week in bCal, or Berkeley Google Calendar.
 
“Personally, I use Google Calendar religiously. I have it set up to notify me when I have classes, discussion sections, Zoom meetings or Google Meets, and any other event. Google Calendar — along with Gmail, Google Docs, and Spotify — is one of the few tabs I always have to have open, just so that I can seamlessly stay organized.” — Joseph, Class of 2029, majoring in philosophy
 
### Berkeley Gmail, AKA bMail
 
Your @berkeley.edu email address is officially known as bMail, but most students just call it their Berkeley email or school email. CalCentral billing notices, campus WarnMe messages, and advising correspondences all go to your bMail inbox, so it’s important to keep it organized.
 
“I sort all of my emails by label so that I can track down specific communications quickly, and so that my inbox doesn’t get clogged. I also regularly go through my starred emails and unstar them after they become irrelevant — for example, after a midterm or important billing date has passed.
 
In addition to my @berkeley.edu email address, I keep three other addresses: an email for personal communications, an email for jobs and internships, and an email for subscriptions. This is helpful for both organization and security purposes.” — Nina, Class of 2026, majoring in film and media
 ![decorative image](https://life.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Nina_s_Labels_EDITED.jpg)
Five of the many, many labels in Nina’s Berkeley email inbox, or bMail.
 
### Planners
 
Almost everyone I know uses some form of planner in addition to their calendar or calendars. These planners track homework assignments, work shifts, club meetings, and everything in between. Here are four different types.
 
**The spreadsheet**
 
“For homework, the almighty spreadsheet is key. Writing down every single assignment, when they’re due, what kind of assignment it is, highlighting and underlining based on priority, is a good way to make sure things don’t slip through the cracks, especially assignments that aren’t on bCourses, or big assignments that need to be started earlier. Cross-referencing this with bCourses is what I do to keep ahead of assignments, and while it’s a hassle to set up and regularly update, it’s a nice little reward to change the dropdown bar from ‘Not started’ to ‘Submitted’ when you finish an assignment.
 
Shoutout to my friend Ryan for suggesting putting due dates earlier than they really are on the homework spreadsheet. It’s a neat trick to help you keep ahead of assignments.” — Nolan, Class of 2027, majoring in media studies
 ![decorative image](https://life.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Nolan_s_Spreadsheet_EDITED.jpg)
Nolan’s homework tracking spreadsheet.
 
**The Google Document**
 
“I absolutely live by my agenda which I keep on a Google Doc. I use bCal to help me visualize my day and big things like classes and meetings, but for the little details like when I need to leave, what to wear, what to bring, etc. — that’s all in my Google Doc. It’s down to the minute and I follow it extremely faithfully. Every weekend I plan out the entire next week this way using my master template and adjusting for each specific day.” — Rachel, Class of 2026, majoring in media studies
 ![decorative image](https://life.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Rachel_s_Google_Doc_EDITED.jpg)
Rachel’s Google Doc weekly planner.
 
**The Notion planner**
 
“I use [Notion](https://www.notion.com/) to keep track of my classwork and readings. It’s a great platform, especially if you have a template from online, and helps me keep track of tasks and not miss deadlines since bCourses doesn’t always give me notifications for things like discussion posts.” — Ethan, Class of 2027, majoring in English
 ![decorative image](https://life.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Ethan_s-Notion-Planner_EDITED.jpg)
Ethan’s Notion planner.
 
“I use Notion to organize my school assignments, and I like to use this as a digital planner where I can set due dates for each smaller assignment, and break up larger tasks into smaller ones. I organize my Notion with a page for each class, and reset it at the beginning of each week with that week’s tasks. I love this platform to keep everything organized!” — Shae, Class of 2029, majoring in English
 
**The old-school planner**
 
“While I primarily use bCal and a digital to do list to keep track of things, I always have a physical planner too. I use it to write down big events like exams, concerts, and flights. Having the same information listed in multiple places means I have reminders all around me. Plus, there’s the added benefit of our brains remembering things better when we write them by hand rather than type them.” — Nina, Class of 2026, majoring in film and media
 ![decorative image](https://life.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Nina_s_Planner_EDITED.jpg)
Nina’s hard-copy calendar.
 
“In addition to using Notion and bCal, I have a whiteboard calendar on my desk. I don’t mark the everyday classes on that — just larger events like big due dates, special events, birthdays, etc.” — Shae, Class of 2029, majoring in English
 
**The mental planner**
 
“Things get busy, so figure out what’s best for you. I’ve learned that no matter how hard I try to plan on paper and in bCal, I honestly still operate best from my head. Planning things out helps me keep my tasks in mind, but I try to be flexible with my scheduling (especially around designating time to complete assignments).” — Milana, Class of 2028, majoring in astrophysics and political science
 
**“**I could never really keep too well to a physical planner or calendar and rely mostly on routine and association instead. I’m a procrastinator, so if I know I need to do something, I set reminders for it earlier than I have to so I have time to ‘get in the mood’ to do it, as it were. I try to associate a task to some other thought or action, so whenever I have that thought, it acts like a lead to my given task.” — Vincent, Class of 2026, majoring in English
 
### Final tips on staying organized
 
Here are some final words of wisdom from current UC Berkeley students.
 
**Schedule in breaks:**“I schedule in time to my days specifically for going through my to-do list or even just taking a break. It’s super easy to get overwhelmed and for things to get ahead of you, so doing this gives me a chance to catch up and feel like I’m on top of things.” — Rachel, Class of 2026, majoring in media studies
 
**Get ahead of your deadlines:** “Though I am by no means great at this, it’s worth trying to get ahead as much as you can during the first part of the semester. Sounds daunting, I know, but even something like being a week or two ahead of readings and homework will ensure you don’t fall behind when midterms come your way, when life happens, and when the burnout starts to creep in at the end of the semester.” — Nolan, Class of 2027, majoring in media studies
 
**Keep a cool head:** “Perhaps this isn’t a real tip, but I find it never helps to stress. Acknowledge the seriousness and importance of a task, but don’t get overwhelmed by it, even if it’s a big one. My dictum has always seemed to be, ‘It has to get done, so it will. Simple as.’” — Vincent, Class of 2026, majoring in English
 
**Double or triple up on methods:** “What works for your friends in terms of organization might not work for you, so don’t be afraid to experiment or double up on methods. I’m a forgetful person, so I normally triple or quadruple up. For example, I put events in my Google Calendar (which is synced to my iPhone’s calendar), my physical Calendar, and my digital to-do list.” — Nina, Class of 2026, majoring in film & media
 
I hope this article introduced you to some new organizational methods, or at least reminded you to have notifications turned on for your calendars and homework assignments. Good luck out there, Golden Bears!
 

 
*Nina Takahashi,**Class of**2026**, is majoring in**film & media**and minoring in Japanese and creative writing. Cover photo by Milana Berhe.*

# Intro to “My Finances” in CalCentral - Life

- **Source URL**: [https://life.berkeley.edu/intro-to-my-finances-in-calcentral/](https://life.berkeley.edu/intro-to-my-finances-in-calcentral/)
- **Crawled At**: 2026-07-16T08:44:31.620Z

## Content

![decorative image](https://life.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Feature-Image-My-Finances_Edited.jpg) 

   By [Nina Takahashi](https://life.berkeley.edu/author/nina-takahashi/) 
 [[Home Berkeley - Life|Copy Link]][[Home Berkeley - Life|Email]][[Home Berkeley - Life|Print]][[Home Berkeley - Life|LinkedIn]]     6 MINUTE READ  Post Views: 219  
  [Fall Start](https://life.berkeley.edu/tag/fall-start/) | [Fin Aid & Scholarships](https://life.berkeley.edu/tag/fin-aid-scholarships/) | [Spring Start](https://life.berkeley.edu/tag/spring-start/)    
## CalCentral explained: the “My Finances” tab
 
In addition to bringing fresh faces and renewed academic vigor, the start of a semester usually entails new charges in CalCentral. CalCentral is UC Berkeley’s comprehensive student portal. It’s the dashboard that students and their delegates use for all of the nitty-gritty: enrolling in classes, updating personal information, and — of course — paying the bills.
 
The aim of this blog is to help you navigate the “My Finances” tab of CalCentral. This tab is where you’ll make payments toward your tuition, but it’s also where you’ll find your financial aid offer, confirm your outside aid, and access useful financial aid resources. There are four sections within My Finances: Tuition Stability Plan, Billing Summary, Financial Aid & Scholarships, and Financial Resources. I cover all of them in detail below.
 
### Tuition Stability Plan
 
This section of My Finances indicates what Tuition Cohort you or your student is assigned to. Under UC Berkeley’s Tuition Stability Plan, all incoming undergraduates (both first-year and transfer students) are assigned to a Tuition Cohort based on the time of their first enrollment at UC Berkeley. The cost of tuition and other mandatory fees are frozen for your given cohort until you graduate or for up to six academic years. Freezing mandatory fees help students and their families understand the relative cost of receiving an undergraduate degree from UC Berkeley.
 
Note that for graduate students, tuition is still adjusted annually based on inflation.
 ![An example Tuition Stability Plan section of My Finances in CalCentral, presenting a student’s assigned undergraduate Tuition Cohort and how long it will remain in effect through.](https://life.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Tuition-Stability-Plan_Edited.jpg)
The Tuition Stability Plan section states which Tuition Cohort you belong to.
 
### Billing Summary
 
The Billing Summary section is where you’ll make payments toward tuition and other mandatory fees. There are multiple parts to this section and I’ve broken down all of them below.
 
- **Due Now:**What mandatory fees, such as tuition, are due at present. Also includes Overdue charges. 
- **View Transactions:** A blue arrow that takes you to a summary of all your transactions, including Unpaid Balance and Payments and Aid. Payments that are not yet due will have a yellow circle and the due date next to them. 
- **Not Yet Due:**What mandatory fees are due in the future. 
- **Total Unpaid Balance:**The total of your Due Now and Not Yet Due charges combined. 
- **Make Payment:** A blue button that links to UC Berkeley’s commerce.cashnet student payment portal, where you can make payments towards mandatory fees, as well as view your transactions, statements, and account details. 
- **View PDF Statement:**Links to the Overview tab of your payment portal, from which you have to navigate to the Statements tab, then click “View” to open a given statement, or click “Save” to download a PDF of the statement.
 
You’ll receive courtesy reminder emails that charges are being billed to your account within the next few days, but be sure to regularly check this section of your CalCentral My Finances so you don’t miss a payment. Missed payments may result in a hold being placed on your CalCentral account.
 ![An example Billing Summary section of My Finances in CalCentral, including a tab where payments can be made and indicating that no charges are due to this student’s account.](https://life.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Billing-Summary_Edited.jpg)
The Billing Summary section is where you’ll find charges due to your account and make payments.
 
### Financial Aid & Scholarships
 
The Financial Aid & Scholarships section is where you’ll view your financial aid package and other related information. It has several subsections that can be a bit confusing to decode, but that’s what this blog is for.
 
**Aid Year:**A toggle button that allows you to choose your aid year. It is set to the current year by default, but you can switch between different years to see what your fees and aid looked like at the time, since your financial aid package may change each year.
 
**Estimated Cost of Attendance:** An estimate of how much one academic year at UC Berkeley costs for you.
 
This number is an estimate established through answers in student surveys and research. It can increase or decrease based on a myriad of factors — whether you enroll in SHIP, whether your professors provide all course materials for free, etc. — but typically includes:
 
- Tuition and fees (assuming full-time attendance) 
- Books, course materials, supplies, and equipment 
- Living expenses (food and housing) 
- Miscellaneous and personal expenses 
- Transportation 
- Health insurance (which can be waived if you’re enrolled in equivalent medical insurance that meets the [University’s requirements](https://uhs.berkeley.edu/insurance-ship/ship-benefits))
 
**Funding Offered:**My personal favorite section, because this is where the dollar amounts of aid from the University and from outside scholarships will appear, reducing your overall tuition. There are subsections which you can toggle open to view what type of aid you’ve received. UC Berkeley Financial Aid & Scholarships [explains the different types of aid in detail](https://financialaid.berkeley.edu/types-of-aid-at-berkeley/), and I’ve included a brief description here.
 
- **Gift Aid:** Comprising scholarships and grants, Gift Aid is awarded from federal, state, and University funds based on financial need and academic merit. It does not need to be repaid. 
- **Outside Resources:**Aid received from third parties, such as scholarship contests and organizations unaffiliated with the University. When your scholarship organization says they’ve sent your award over to UC Berkeley, this is the section where you’ll double check that. 
- **Waivers:** Expenses that are covered through waivers. If you waive the Student Health Insurance Plan (SHIP) because you are already enrolled in an approved private health insurance, then the dollar amount of SHIP will show up in this section and be deducted from your tuition. 
- Note: The timing of when you waive out of SHIP can impact the financial aid you receive. For example, if you are granted a SHIP waiver after your aid has disbursed, your awards may be reduced to account for the SHIP waiver. Refer to [SHIP FAQs](https://financialaid.berkeley.edu/how-aid-works/student-health-insurance-plan-ship-faq/) to learn more. 
- **Loans:** A sum of money you borrow from a lender and pay back over time, with interest added. Subsidized loans are available to undergraduate students who demonstrate financial need and the U.S. Department of Education pays the interest on them. Unsubsidized loans are available to both undergraduate and graduate students regardless of need and the student is responsible for paying the interest on them. CalCentral will indicate which type of loan is available to you. 
- Note: You may be able to convert any federal loans into work-study funds. 
- **Work-Study:** A part-time paid campus job, the salary of which goes toward your tuition. A dollar amount will appear next to work-study if you are eligible for it. We have several blogs about [how to apply to work-study positions](https://life.berkeley.edu/work-study-how-to-apply/). Writing blogs like this for Berkeley Life was initially a work-study job for me, and I’m so grateful I found it.
 ![An example Financial Aid & Scholarships section of My Finances in CalCentral, including work-study and other gift aid funding offered.](https://life.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Financial-Aid-Scholarship-Blocked_Edited.jpg)
Financial Aid & Scholarships details the types of financial aid available to you. My first year at Cal, I received $4,700 from outside resources through essay-based scholarships.
 
### Financial Resources
 
This is a helpful compilation of resources to help you understand and manage your finances. You can enroll in UCB Direct Deposit, which allows you to electronically receive disbursements to your bank account from UC Berkeley. You can also view your Tax 1098-T Form, which is issued by UC Berkeley to students and which you may be able to use to claim a tax credit. Delegate Access links to your Student Profile, where you can add “delegates,” or individuals who can act on you or your student’s behalf to pay bills, view your academic information, and more. Delegates are typically your guardians. You can add funds to your Cal 1 Card debit account to pay for select services on campus, such as printing at some libraries. You can also check on your meal plan balance.
 ![An example Financial Resources section of My Finances in CalCentral, including hyperlinks to Direct Deposit management and the 1098-T tax form.](https://life.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Financial-Resources_Edited.jpg)
Financial Resources provides quick access to various resources, including your Direct Deposit account and 1098-T tax form.
 
### Conclusion
 
I hope this blog offered you some insight into the comprehensive resource hub that is the My Finances tab of your student’s CalCentral dashboard. Before we part, I offer one last piece of advice about My Finances: Enroll in UCB Direct Deposit! It eliminates the hassle of paper checks if you work a work-study job and in the event that you receive a reimbursement from the University.
 
Good luck this semester, Golden Bears!
 

 
*Nina Takahashi**,**Class of**2026**, is majoring in**film & media**and minoring in Japanese and creative writing*. *Cover photo by Student Affairs Communications.*
 
**Want more?**
 
- Get a student’s perspective on [how to manage your finances](https://life.berkeley.edu/managing-your-finances/). 
- Discover the [joys of working on campus](https://life.berkeley.edu/golden-bears-at-work/). 
- Learn [6 financial aid tips](https://life.berkeley.edu/6-financial-aid-tips/) from a financial aid expert.

# Privacy Statement for UC Berkeley Websites Office of Ethics, Risk, and Compliance Services

- **Source URL**: [https://security.berkeley.edu/privacy-statement-uc-berkeley-websites](https://security.berkeley.edu/privacy-statement-uc-berkeley-websites)
- **Crawled At**: 2026-07-16T08:44:31.626Z

## Content

Responsible Executive   Responsible Office    Contact UC Berkeley Privacy Office, [privacyoffice@berkeley.edu(link sends e-mail)](mailto:privacyoffice@berkeley.edu)      
Effective Date: April 2009
Latest revision: June 2020
 
For questions about this Standard, contact: [UC Berkeley Privacy Office(link is external)](http://privacy.berkeley.edu/)
  
## Standard
 
- The University of California, Berkeley is committed to protecting the privacy and accuracy of your confidential information to the extent possible, subject to provisions of state and federal law. Other than as required by laws that guarantee public access to certain types of information, or in response to subpoenas or other legal instruments that authorize access, personally-identifiable information is not actively shared. In particular, we do not re-distribute or sell personal information collected on our web servers.
 
## Information collected
 
- UC Berkeley websites may collect personal information such as name, address, e-mail address, telephone number(s), and/or educational interests. Such personal information may be requested by us for research, public service or teaching programs, or for administrative purposes. Additional personal information, such as credit card account information, may be requested for purchases or enrollment purposes. 
- Web servers typically collect, at least temporarily, the following information: Internet Protocol (IP) address of computer being used; web pages requested; referring web page; browser used; date and time. UC Berkeley may collect statistics identifying particular IP addresses from which our websites are accessed.
 
## Use of collected information
 
- UC Berkeley may use personal information collected from websites for the purpose of future communication back to online enrollees, in order to keep you informed of such activities as campus programs, symposia and/or special events, but only if you are provided the opportunity to opt out of that type of use. 
- UC Berkeley may use browser-IP-address information and anonymous-browser history to report information about site accesses and for profiling purposes. This information is generally used to improve Web presentation and utilization. The campus also may use IP address information for troubleshooting purposes. 
- Some UC Berkeley online activity sites may use "cookies" in order to deliver web content specific to individual users’ interests or to keep track of online purchasing transactions. Sensitive personal information is not stored within cookies. 
- Also see the Berkeley Office of Ethics [Online Monitoring web page(link is external)(link is external)](https://ethics.berkeley.edu/privacy/online-monitoring)
 
## Distribution of collected information
 
- UC Berkeley will not disclose, without your consent, personal information collected about you, except for certain explicit circumstances in which disclosure is required by law. 
- UC Berkeley will not distribute or sell personal information to third-party organizations.
 
## Individual choice
 
- Individuals who wish to use methods other than online enrollment may submit requests by email or U.S. mail addressed to the UC Berkeley organization responsible for the website.
 
## Access to own information
 
- Questions regarding users’ rights to review, modify or delete their previously provided personal information should be directed to the campus organization to which they provided the information. Any disputes will be resolved under existing records regulations applicable to UC Berkeley.
 
## Additional Information
 
- For more detailed information about requirements for campus online activities see the [Campus Online Activities Policy section on Privacy and Confidentiality of Information(link is external)](https://security.berkeley.edu/policy/online#priv).
 
## Responsibility for external sites
 
- UC Berkeley does not control the content or information practices of external organizations. We recommend you review the privacy statements of these organizations.
 
## General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)
 If you are accessing this site from a country that is a member of the European Union (EU), the European Economic Area (EAA), or the United Kingdom (UK), the processing of your Personal Data is subject to the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the UK GDPR, or other European Privacy laws. UC Berkeley complies with the requirements of GDPR, the UK GDPR, and other European privacy laws. For information regarding your rights under European privacy laws, including the GDPR and UK GDPR; and/or UC Berkeley’s compliance with their requirements, refer to the [UC Berkeley Privacy Office’s GDPR site;(link is external)(link is external)](https://ethics.berkeley.edu/privacy/general-data-protection-regulation-gdpr) or contact the UC Berkeley Privacy office: privacyoffice@berkeley.edu or (510) 664-7775.

# Report a web accessibility issue Digital Accessibility

- **Source URL**: [https://dap.berkeley.edu/get-help/report-web-accessibility-issue](https://dap.berkeley.edu/get-help/report-web-accessibility-issue)
- **Crawled At**: 2026-07-16T08:44:31.626Z

## Content

## Reporting Accessibility Issues
 
To report an accessibility barrier with UC Berkeley's online content, please complete the form, **[Report a web accessibility issue(link is external)](https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdWVlD0HOsQuvmDTsJiwrKEhpI_o3dd_tIbnXpy_8_Gp1vGzw/viewform)**. This includes accessibility barriers on websites or BerkeleyX courses, captions on videos, and transcripts for podcasts. For more information on the kinds of content that are covered by this form, please review “[What is the process for public requests for accessibility?](https://dap.berkeley.edu/policy-and-procedure/web-accessibility-procedures#whatisprocess)”
 
If you’ve encountered barriers for different types of content, please submit more than one report.
 
## Web Accessibility Procedures
 
Please refer to the [Web Accessibility Procedures](https://dap.berkeley.edu/policy-and-procedure/web-accessibility-procedures) for guidance on publicly available websites and BerkeleyX courses as well as audio and video content under the Consent Decree with the US Department of Justice.
 
## IT Accessibility Policy
 
The University seeks to deploy information technology that has been designed, developed, or procured to be accessible to people with disabilities, including those who use assistive technologies. For more details, please refer to our [Information Technology Accessibility Policy(link is external)](https://policy.ucop.edu/doc/7000611/IMT-1300).

35da484e90cc3f60.title: Undergrad Living Perspective - Life
35da484e90cc3f60.content:
# Undergrad Living Perspective - Life

- **Source URL**: [https://life.berkeley.edu/undergrad-living-perspective/](https://life.berkeley.edu/undergrad-living-perspective/)
- **Crawled At**: 2026-07-16T08:44:31.608Z

## Content

![decorative image](https://life.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Res-perspective-collage.jpg) 

   By [Ethan Teeguarden](https://life.berkeley.edu/author/eteegers13/) 
 [[Home Berkeley - Life|Copy Link]][[Home Berkeley - Life|Email]][[Home Berkeley - Life|Print]][[Home Berkeley - Life|LinkedIn]]     5 MINUTE READ  Post Views: 40  
  [Housing & Dining](https://life.berkeley.edu/tag/housing-dining/)    
## **My undergraduate living experiences for two years in campus housing**
 
Starting at UC Berkeley, I had no idea what to expect before moving into the residence halls as a first-year. I had never visited the city and only knew what the residence halls looked like from the [UC Berkeley Housing website](https://housing.berkeley.edu/) and Google Maps. I ended up having the chance to live in on-campus housing for two years: one year at Blackwell Hall and Foothill, and the other year at xučyun ruwway in Albany.
 
One experience that helped me tremendously in acclimating to Berkeley was taking a semester of classes before my first year through the [Summer Bridge program](https://slc.berkeley.edu/summer-bridge). I got to learn what living in a residence hall would be like in a less busy environment than the fall and spring semesters when campus is a bustling place. During the summer program, I lived in [Blackwell Hall](https://housing.berkeley.edu/explore-housing-options/residence-halls/blackwell-hall/) for six weeks before moving to my assigned campus residence hall, [Foothill](https://housing.berkeley.edu/explore-housing-options/residence-halls/foothill-unit-4/), for my fall and spring semesters.
 ![decorative image](https://life.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Ethan_blackwell_EDITED.jpg)
My partner and I moving into Blackwell Hall for the six-week Summer Bridge program.
 
### **Living in a residence hall mini-suite**
 
During my first year, I lived in a mini-suite in the La Loma section of Foothill, where I had one roommate and seven suitemates. I had a random roommate situation, and while my roommate and I never got to be close friends, I found a community through my Golden Bear Orientation (GBO) group that included a few of my suitemates.
 
Living in a suite with more than just two rooms offers an experience similar to traditional residence halls in that it is essentially one big hallway with a closer group of friends. We kept our doors open often and socialized in our common space. [Roommate](https://housing.berkeley.edu/living-on-campus/living-with-a-roommate/) and suite agreement forms were essential to knowing boundaries and expectations, and it is something myself and my livingmates took seriously during our first year.
 ![decorative image](https://life.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Ethan_foothill_EDITED.jpg)
My freshman year room in a Foothill suite.
 
Foothill was different from my initial experience in Blackwell. Mainly, my room in Foothill offered more space to move around and the common area in my minisuite was spacious. While Blackwell has many comfortable lounges on each floor, I enjoyed having a common space right outside my door. I bought a small TV for the space that everyone in the suite used to watch movies or shows, and that helped make the space feel like a home.
 
The distance between Foothill and main campus buildings can be daunting at first, especially considering the large incline on the way back from campus. The location also gives Foothill a more quiet environment compared to the dorms south of campus, and it is actually much closer to campus buildings for STEM classes. The long walks helped me become familiar with the campus in my first year, and when I wasn’t feeling up for the walk I was able to learn the [Bear Transit](https://pt.berkeley.edu/public-transportation/bear-transit) bus system for going back and forth between class and my dorm.
 
### **Living in an apartment**
 
During my second year, I chose to live in campus housing again, and while I was initially assigned a Unit 3 double room, I received an email with an offer to live in a four-bedroom, two-bathroom campus apartment at the brand new graduate housing building [xučyun ruwway](https://housing.berkeley.edu/explore-housing-options/apartments/xucyun-ruwway-apartments/) in Albany, next to UC Berkeley’s family housing community, [University Village](https://housing.berkeley.edu/explore-housing-options/family-student-housing-university-village/).
 
[Note: Undergraduate students who are not first-year students (freshmen) are now eligible to live in shared apartments at xučyun ruwway. They live in a separate building from graduate students but share common amenities such as the gym, lobby, common areas, etc.]
 
The brand new building offered modern amenities and a single bedroom, offering a more private space than the traditional Unit 3 residence halls. The only challenge for me was the distance from campus, which requires a 20- to 30-minute bus ride to and from the UC Berkeley campus.
 
Here are the main takeaways from my year living in xučyun ruwway as an undergraduate:
 
**What went into my decision to live at xučyun ruwway?**
 
xučyun ruwway offered a single bedroom apartment in a brand new building — I was a part of the first cohort living there. I had financial aid that helped me cover the monthly payments; in my case, the payments included all utilities and amenities, but not a meal plan.
 
Overall, I preferred living in a more private, apartment-style space over living at a Unit 3 residence hall, and I was ready to take on the experience of living in an apartment, including cooking and cleaning on my own.
 
**What amenities did I find useful?**
 
xučyun ruwway offers incredible amenities. The on-site gym has 24-hour access with multiple machines available for use. There is a plethora of study space located near the lobby and on each floor, and the mailroom has easy and secure access with a phone app. The main thing I miss from my time living at xučyun ruwway now that I live off campus is the free laundry in each apartment. Laundry can get expensive, but each individual apartment there had a washer and dryer with no payments required.
 ![decorative image](https://life.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/EDITED_260407_Undergrad_Living_in_Grad_Housing_Photos_Collage-3.jpg)
xučyun ruwway is a very modern style apartment building, with many amenities and lots of space within the apartments. These are some common spaces in the lobby, a look inside the apartments, and the greenery outside. Photos courtesy of Student Affairs Communications.
 
**How was it different from other campus housing?**
 
With my experience living in Blackwell Hall and Foothill in mind, the main difference was the commute to campus every day. Taking the 52 or 18 bus line to campus meant I needed to plan ahead of time or I would essentially miss my entire class — this did happen quite often. I also worked late nights during the spring semester that year, and I would sometimes need to take an Uber home since the 52 and 18 bus lines would stop running late at nights on weekends.
 
I also had to adapt to not having a meal plan, which meant cooking for myself often. I signed up for [CalFresh food benefits](https://basicneeds.berkeley.edu/calfresh), which helped me buy groceries at a nearby Sprouts, Whole Foods, or Safeway in Albany. University Village also has a [food pantry](https://gradfamilyliving.berkeley.edu/family-living-university-village/university-village/bear-pantry/) with fresh produce weekly right outside the xučyun ruwway apartment complex for folks in need of food assistance.
 
**How did I find a community?**
 
While I lived in an area with predominantly graduate students, the UC Village area has a thriving community of families and students to interact with. I went to the [University Village Community Center](https://recwell.berkeley.edu/facilities/university-village-community-center/) to play basketball almost every Tuesday or Thursday night, and I found a group of friendly residents who welcomed me into their community immediately. I saw the same people almost every week there and I still return to Albany occasionally to play basketball with that group of people even though I live in an off-campus apartment now.
 
### **My takeaways from campus housing**
 
I think it’s safe to say that I have had a unique experience in my over two years in campus housing. I lived in three different styles of housing: a traditional residence hall at Blackwell, a suite at Foothill, and an apartment at xučyun ruwway. Overall, I tried to make the most of the amenities and community spaces in campus housing, whether it be social lounges or community recreation. I hope that my experience can help others gauge what they want from their undergraduate living experience and how to navigate the shared spaces.
 

 
**Ethan Teeguarden**,**Class of**2027**, is majoring in**English**and minoring in**journalism**. Cover photo courtesy of Student Affairs Communications*.*
 
**Want more?**
 
- A guide to [all things Berkeley housing](https://life.berkeley.edu/housing-start-here/) for incoming students. 
- Are you a graduate student? Find out about [campus grad housing options](https://life.berkeley.edu/grad-housing-student-perspectives/). 
- How you can [find your community](https://life.berkeley.edu/community-in-campus-housing/) through campus housing.

# Frequently Asked Questions - Reading & Composition Requirement College Writing Programs

- **Source URL**: [https://writing.berkeley.edu/faq/reading-composition-requirement](https://writing.berkeley.edu/faq/reading-composition-requirement)
- **Crawled At**: 2026-07-16T13:52:36.034Z

## Content

## Reading & Composition Requirement
 [collapse all](#openberkeley-expand-all-0) [expand all](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-0-target)      
### [Can I satisfy the Reading & Composition 1A Requirement at a California Community College (CCC)?](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-0-target)
   Before starting coursework at Berkeley, you can satisfy the R&C 1A Requirement at most community colleges as long as the course has been certified by UC Berkeley as satisfying the R&C 1A Requirement. You must earn a grade of C or higher to satisfy the requirement. Make sure the CCC sends your transcript to the Admissions Office at Berkeley.    
After you have started coursework at Berkeley, you cannot take a course at a CCC to satisfy the R&C 1A Requirement.
         
### [I failed COLWRIT R1A. Can I retake the course in the summer at a California Community College?](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-1-target)
   No. You must do the coursework at a UC campus.      
### [Can I satisfy the UC Entry-Level Writing Requirement and the R&C 1A Requirement in one semester?](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-2-target)
   UC Berkeley offers one course that satisfies both requirements at the same time: COLWRIT R1A.    
Other UC campuses require you to complete a 2-course sequence to satisfy both requirements. The courses cannot be taken concurrently. Contact an advisor in your college here at Berkeley, or contact the other campuses directly for further information.
         
### [I failed COLWRIT R1A. Can I retake the course in the summer at another UC campus?](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-3-target)
   If you fail COLWRIT R1A, you must retake COLWRIT R1A to eliminate the failing grade on your transcript.       
### [What's the difference between COLWRIT R1A and COLWRIT R4A?](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-4-target)
   COLWRIT R1A is the 6-unit course that satisfies both the entry level writing requirement and the first half of the reading and composition requirement. COLWRIT R4A is a 4-unit course for students who have already satisfied the ELWR. It satisfies the first half of the reading and composition requirement.

f56bc248f8ef320c.path: expand_task_1784209956117/Frequently Asked Questions - COLWRIT R1A College Writing Programs.md
f56bc248f8ef320c.content:
# Frequently Asked Questions - COLWRIT R1A College Writing Programs

- **Source URL**: [https://writing.berkeley.edu/faq/colwrit-r1a](https://writing.berkeley.edu/faq/colwrit-r1a)
- **Crawled At**: 2026-07-16T13:52:46.586Z

## Content

## COLWRIT R1A
 [collapse all](#openberkeley-expand-all-0) [expand all](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-0-target)      
### [What is COLWRIT R1A?](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-0-target)
   COLWRIT R1A, Accelerated Reading and Composition, is an intensive 6-unit seminar that concurrently satisfies the University of California Entry-Level Writing Requirement and the first part of the University's two-part Reading & Composition Requirement.      
### [What will I do in COLWRIT R1A?](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-1-target)
   Students read imaginative, expository, and argumentative texts representative of the range of those encountered in the undergraduate curriculum. Readings feature authors from diverse social and cultural backgrounds and perspectives. Additionally, students are instructed in techniques for writing a range of discourse forms, and in the revision of papers. In response to course readings and instruction in technique, students write short (2-3 pages) and longer (4-6 pages) essays. Other writing assignments may include journals, quickwrites, reflections, or text responses. The students' writing serves as a text in the class as well, and papers are frequently revised through multiple drafts.      
### [What is the format of the class?](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-2-target)
   Class size is limited to 14. The class is an interactive seminar; student discussion and writing are at the center.      
### [Is there a final examination?](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-3-target)
   No. The culminating project for all COLWRIT R1A students is preparing a portfolio.      
### [How are COLWRIT R1A portfolios graded?](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-4-target)
   
Each student's portfolio is read by a College Writing lecturer that is not the student's instructor. It is marked as passing or not passing according to scoring guidelines developed by College Writing Programs.
      
### [What if I disagree with my portfolio's grade? Can I talk to the instructor who rated it?](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-5-target)
   
You will receive a detailed statement from your rater as to why your portfolio didn't pass. If you disagree with this, you should speak to your own instructor. We do not release the names of raters to students.
      
### [I should have gotten a C-, but instead I got a D+. Why?](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-6-target)
   
In order to pass R1A, you must receive a C or better. While a C- is a failing grade in this course, if you receive a C- you must repeat the course but *cannot replace the C- grade.* With a D+, you still need to retake the course, but your new grade will replace the D+ in your GPA.
      
### [Where can I go if I want extra help with my writing?](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-7-target)
   The Student Learning Center (SLC), located in the Cesar Chavez Center in lower Sproul, offers peer tutors who are trained to work with students on their writing. In addition, SLC offers tutoring in a broad range of courses.       
### [How do I enroll in COLWRIT R1A?](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-8-target)
   The same way you enroll in any other class using CalCentral. There are often waiting lists for this class, so try to enroll as early as you can.      
### [When should I take COLWRIT R1A?](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-9-target)
   You should take COLWRIT R1A in your freshman year.      
### [Which section should I enroll in?](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-10-target)
   Each section has its own theme and reading list. See the descriptions of COLWRIT R1A sections being offered in the upcoming semester, and choose the one that interests you the most.      
### [Should I enroll in a section for multilingual speakers of English?](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-11-target)
   Some COLWRIT R1A sections are reserved for students who are fluent in languages other than English. If your Analytical Writing Placement Exam results suggest that you would benefit from specialized instruction, or if you want a chance to learn more about the structure of English while you read and write, consider enrolling in one of these sections.       
### [What do I do if I can't get into the course this semester?](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-12-target)
   The College Writing Programs (CWP) will may every effort to reserve a space for you the following semester.      
### [Can I enroll in COLWRIT R1A if I have already fulfilled the UC Entry Level Writing Requirement and/or R&C Requirement?](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-13-target)
   Only under extreme circumstances, but generally no. Contact [collegewriting@berkeley.edu(link sends e-mail)](mailto:collegewriting@berkeley.edu) to explain your situation.      
### [What course do I take after COLWRIT R1A to fulfill the second half of the R&C requirement?](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-14-target)
   
UC Berkeley offers courses in a wide range of departments that fulfill the second half of the R&C requirement (see, for example, COLWRIT R4B). Check the [Schedule of Classes(link is external)](http://classes.berkeley.edu/) to find out which courses are currently being offered.
      
### [Can I enroll in COLWRIT R1A if I haven't satisfied the ELWR?](#openberkeley-collapsible-container-15-target)
   Yes.

# Reading and Composition UC Berkeley Catalog

- **Source URL**: [https://undergraduate.catalog.berkeley.edu/earning-your-degree/college-school-requirements/reading-composition](https://undergraduate.catalog.berkeley.edu/earning-your-degree/college-school-requirements/reading-composition)
- **Crawled At**: 2026-07-16T13:52:53.183Z

## Content

## **Guidelines for Reading and Composition Courses**

In order to provide a solid foundation in reading, writing, and critical thinking for work in the major, the College requires two semesters of lower division work in composition—Reading and Composition (R&C), Parts A and B, in sequential order.

- All undergraduates should complete the Reading and Composition (R&C) requirement by the end of their fourth semester.
- All courses used to satisfy Part A or B of Reading and Composition must be completed with a letter grade of C- or better.
- Students who have been admitted to Berkeley and have not completed [Entry Level Writing](http://guide.berkeley.edu/undergraduate/colleges-schools/letters-science/entry-level-writing-requirement/) must enroll in College Writing R1A (6 units), which satisfies both Entry Level Writing and the first half of R&C. Please note: A minimum grade of C is required in COLWRIT R1A in order to satisfy the Entry Level Writing Requirement.
- AGRS R44 (completed with a C- or higher) may be used to satisfy either Part A or Part B of R&C. This course may also be used to satisfy Arts and Literature, Historical Studies, or Social & Behavioral Sciences breadth.
- With the exception of AGRS R44, courses fulfilling the Reading and Composition requirement may not be applied to[Seven-Course Breadth](https://lsadvising.berkeley.edu/seven-course-breadth).

### **Satisfying Reading and Composition with an Exam**

- Advanced Placement (AP) English Literature and Composition - Minimum Score of 4 satisfies Part A
- Advanced Placement (AP) English Literature and Composition - Minimum Score of 5 satisfies Parts A & B
- Advanced Placement (AP) English Language and Composition - Score of 4 or 5 satisfies Part A
- International Baccalaureate (IB) Higher Level (HL) English A: Literature* - Score of 5, 6, or 7 satisfies Parts A & B
- *Beginning with students admitted in fall 2018* - International Baccalaureate (IB) Higher Level (HL) English A: Language and Literature* - Score of 5, 6, or 7 satisfies Parts A & B
- GCE A-Level English Literature exam *- Not accepted for this requirement*

* The IB *Literature and Performance exam*, as well as the Standard Level (SL) exams in *English A: Literature* and *English A: Language and Literature* are NOT eligible for satisfaction of Reading and Composition.

### **Satisfying Reading and Composition with Berkeley Courses**

- Successful completion with a C- grade or better of two designated Reading and Composition courses in sequence order. Review all approved below.

### **Satisfying Reading and Composition Requirement with Transfer Courses**

- Transfer courses must be taken on a letter-graded basis and be completed with a grade of C- or better.
- Students admitted with full CalGETC/UC IGETC Certification from a California Community College (CCC) or UC Reciprocity to the colleges of Chemistry, Computing, Data Science & Society, Education, Environmental Design, Letters & Science, and Rausser Natural Resources, as well as the School of Education, have satisfied Reading and Composition. No additional coursework is required.
- Students can complete an articulated (pre-approved) Reading and Composition course at a CCC. Pre-approved courses can be found on[ASSIST](http://www.assist.org/web-assist/welcome.html).
- Current pre-approved Reading and Composition courses from outside of the California Community College System are published on the [Transfer Evaluation System website](https://tes.collegesource.com/publicview/TES_publicview01.aspx?rid=a10a4846-fc9e-4eaf-bda8-6f72fbaab662&aid=fe2fa5fd-3cef-4d0a-a023-7e47c8fe259b).

It is advisable to refer to individual college/school advising websites regarding use of transfer courses before enrolling elsewhere to complete degree requirements.

## Content

## **Entry-Level Writing and the Berkeley Writing Assessment**
 
### Results from the May 16, 2026 BWA are in students' [CalCentral(link is external)](https://calcentral.berkeley.edu) dashboard under My Academics.
 
### If you missed the May BWA, the makeup will be offered from September 2026. Check this webpage in August to sign up.
 
The UC Entry Level Writing Requirement (ELWR) is a reading and writing proficiency requirement. It is a prerequisite to the Reading and Composition (R&C) requirement. R&C is a two-part (A & B) college-level reading and writing requirement assigned to all Berkeley undergraduates. Check the [Berkeley Guide(link is external)](https://guide.berkeley.edu/undergraduate/colleges-schools/) to review information from your college for more details.
 
All first-year students entering UC should fulfill the Entry Level Writing Requirement by the end of their first year of enrollment at Berkeley. The ELWR may be satisfied with a [qualifying test score(link is external)](https://admission.universityofcalifornia.edu/elwr/), a college-level English composition course taken before starting at Berkeley, or a passing score on the Berkeley Writing Assessment.
 
- Make-up sessions will be available beginning in September. 
- You may complete the assessment only once.
 
After completing the BWA, a $196 fee will be added to your Billing Summary under My Finances on your CalCentral dashboard. If you previously qualified for the UC Application fee waiver, it will be automatically applied.
 
Please read through the Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) below for answers to your general questions.
  
### I have another question about the Assessment. Who do I contact?
 
You can email College Writing Programs at [collegewriting@berkeley.edu(link sends e-mail)](mailto:collegewriting@berkeley.edu) or call the front desk at 510-642-5570.

# Berkeley Writing Assessment Exams College Writing Programs

- **Source URL**: [https://writing.berkeley.edu/topics/berkeley-writing-assessment-exams](https://writing.berkeley.edu/topics/berkeley-writing-assessment-exams)
- **Crawled At**: 2026-07-16T13:58:02.819Z

## Content

## [Berkeley Writing Assessment](/news/berkeley-writing-assessment)
  May 21, 2026
The results of the Berkeley Writing Assessment will be released in approximately 3 weeks.
 
Information about the makeup dates will be available later this summer.
 
Makeup assessments will be available beginning September 2026.
  
- [Read more about Berkeley Writing Assessment](/news/berkeley-writing-assessment)
     
## [Is the digital SAT approved to meet the Entry Level Writing Requirement (ELWR)?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment-exams/digital-sat-approved-meet-entry-level-writing-requirement-elwr)
  
No, unfortunately the digital SAT is not approved to meet the Entry Level Writing Requirement (ELWR).
  
- [Read more about Is the digital SAT approved to meet the Entry Level Writing Requirement (ELWR)?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment-exams/digital-sat-approved-meet-entry-level-writing-requirement-elwr)
     
## [I am waiting on an AP or IB score - why should I consider taking the Assessment in May?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment-exams/i-am-waiting-ap-or-ib-score-why-should-i-consider-taking)
  
If you are interested in enrolling in an Reading and Composition course during the fall semester, then satisfaction of Entry Level Writing must be confirmed before the start of enrollment in mid-July. It may be to your advantage to take the Assessment in the annual May date as a back-up in case you do not receive the minimum score needed on your AP or IB exam.
 
If you decide not to take the Assessment in May, and you do not receive a qualifying AP or IB exam score, you can still take a make-up Assessment during the fall semester and...
  
- [Read more about I am waiting on an AP or IB score - why should I consider taking the Assessment in May?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment-exams/i-am-waiting-ap-or-ib-score-why-should-i-consider-taking)
     
## [Will my Advanced Placement (AP) or International Baccalaureate (IB) course I completed in high school satisfy the Entry Level Writing Requirement if I haven't taken the exam?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment-exams/will-my-advanced-placement-ap-or-international-baccalaureate)
  
No, an AP or IB course alone will not satisfy the ELWR. You must have an acceptable score on these exams to meet the ELWR. You can view acceptable exam scores on the [University of California ELWR website(link is external)](https://admission.universityofcalifornia.edu/elwr/).
  
- [Read more about Will my Advanced Placement (AP) or International Baccalaureate (IB) course I completed in high school satisfy the Entry Level Writing Requirement if I haven't taken the exam?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment-exams/will-my-advanced-placement-ap-or-international-baccalaureate)
     
## [Can I use scores from the Test of English as a Foreign Language (TOEFL), the International English Language Testing System (IELTS), or Duolingo English Test (DET) to satisfy the ELWR?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment-exams/can-i-use-scores-test-english-foreign-language-toefl)
  
No, not for the Entry Level Writing Requirement. TOEFL, IELTS, or DET scores may be used to demonstrate [English language proficiency(link is external)](https://admission.universityofcalifornia.edu/admission-requirements/international-applicants/english-language-proficiency-toefl-ielts.html), but are not acceptable for the ELWR.
 
You can see which exams may be used to satisfy the ELWR on the [UC ELWR website(link is external)](https://admission.universityofcalifornia.edu/elwr/).
  
- [Read more about Can I use scores from the Test of English as a Foreign Language (TOEFL), the International English Language Testing System (IELTS), or Duolingo English Test (DET) to satisfy the ELWR?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment-exams/can-i-use-scores-test-english-foreign-language-toefl)
     
## [Can I use my Smarter Balanced score to satisfy ELWR?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment-exams/can-i-use-my-smarter-balanced-score-satisfy-elwr)
  
No. The Smarter Balanced score is used by some campuses as an *additional* piece of information for placement into courses. UC Berkeley does not currently use the Smarter Balanced Assessment.
  
- [Read more about Can I use my Smarter Balanced score to satisfy ELWR?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment-exams/can-i-use-my-smarter-balanced-score-satisfy-elwr)
     
## [How and where do I send my exam scores to satisfy the Entry Level Writing Requirement (ELWR)?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment-exams/how-and-where-do-i-send-my-exam-scores-satisfy-entry-level)
  
If you intend to use an exam score to satisfy the ELWR, you must request that your official scores be sent to Berkeley via the testing agency's website as soon as all of your scores are available to make sure they're received in time. Be sure to use the college code 0444 for the ACT and 4833 for the SAT.
  
- [Read more about How and where do I send my exam scores to satisfy the Entry Level Writing Requirement (ELWR)?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment-exams/how-and-where-do-i-send-my-exam-scores-satisfy-entry-level)
     
## [I am confused about ACT Scores. How do they count?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment-exams/i-am-confused-about-act-scores-how-do-they-count)
  On the ELWR webpage, it says the following: “Score 30 or better on ACT English Language Arts, or 63 or better on ACT English + Reading” in order to satisfy the ELWR. But in the next section, it also says that “The ACT English alone will not fulfill the ELWR.” What does that mean?
There are two types of ACT scores: a score on English Language Arts (ELA) which is given if you complete the optional Writing test; and another score on English + Reading if you do not complete the optional Writing test.
 
If you have an ELA score, you will need a 30 or better to meet the ELWR.
 
If you have an English + Reading score, you will need a combined score (a sum of the English and Reading scores) of 63 or better to meet the ELWR*. The combined score must be from a single sitting, in other words, from the same exam.* You cannot combine scores from multiple exam...
  
- [Read more about I am confused about ACT Scores. How do they count?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment-exams/i-am-confused-about-act-scores-how-do-they-count)

# Berkeley Writing Assessment General Questions College Writing Programs

- **Source URL**: [https://writing.berkeley.edu/topics/berkeley-writing-assessment-general-questions](https://writing.berkeley.edu/topics/berkeley-writing-assessment-general-questions)
- **Crawled At**: 2026-07-16T13:58:09.560Z

## Content

## [Berkeley Writing Assessment](/berkeley-writing-assessment)
  **Entry-Level Writing and the Berkeley Writing Assessment** Results from the May 16, 2026 BWA are in students' [CalCentral(link is external)](https://calcentral.berkeley.edu) dashboard under My Academics.  If you missed the May BWA, the makeup will be offered from September 2026. Check this webpage in August to sign up. 
The UC Entry Level Writing Requirement (ELWR) is a reading and writing proficiency requirement. It is a prerequisite to the Reading and Composition (R&C) requirement. R&C is a two-part (A...
  
- [Read more about Berkeley Writing Assessment](/berkeley-writing-assessment)
     
## [I took the BWA. How long will it be until I get my score?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment-general-questions/i-took-bwa-how-long-will-it-be-until-i-get-my)
  
It generally takes around 3 weeks for your essay to be scored and for the score to be submitted before it appears in your records. You can find your BWA scores on your [Cal Central(link is external)](https://calcentral.berkeley.edu/) dashboard under "Degree Progress". You can see your score, and your ELWR will now show as satisfied if you earned a score of 8 or higher.
  
- [Read more about I took the BWA. How long will it be until I get my score?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment-general-questions/i-took-bwa-how-long-will-it-be-until-i-get-my)
     
## [Berkeley Writing Assessment](/news/berkeley-writing-assessment)
  May 21, 2026
The results of the Berkeley Writing Assessment will be released in approximately 3 weeks.
 
Information about the makeup dates will be available later this summer.
 
Makeup assessments will be available beginning September 2026.
  
- [Read more about Berkeley Writing Assessment](/news/berkeley-writing-assessment)
     
## [Structure and Scoring of the Assessment](/berkeley-writing-assessment/structure-and-scoring-assessment)
  The Structure of the Assessment 
You'll begin by reading a prose passage of 700-1,000 words. This passage will be about as difficult as the readings in first-year courses at UC Berkeley. You'll have up to two hours to read the passage carefully and write an essay in response to a single topic and related questions based on the passage's content. These questions will generally ask you to read thoughtfully and to provide reasoned, concrete, and developed presentations of a specific point of view. Your essay will be evaluated on the basis of your ability to develop your central idea, to...
  
- [Read more about Structure and Scoring of the Assessment](/berkeley-writing-assessment/structure-and-scoring-assessment)
     
## [How much does the Berkeley Writing Assessment cost?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment-general-questions/how-much-does-berkeley-writing-assessment-cost)
  
Upon completing the BWA, a $196 fee will be charged and applied to your Billing Summary account under My Finances in your CalCentral dashboard. Payment is due by Friday, May 30, 2025. If you previously qualified for the UC Application fee waiver, an automatic fee waiver will be applied.
  
- [Read more about How much does the Berkeley Writing Assessment cost?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment-general-questions/how-much-does-berkeley-writing-assessment-cost)
     
## [Example of an Assessment Topic](/berkeley-writing-assessment/example-assessment-topic)
  
Below is an example of an assessment reading and question in the style you can expect for the BWA.
 Directions Read the passage and the essay topic that follows. Respond to the topic by writing an essay that is controlled by a central idea and is developed by discussing specific examples. You will have two hours to read the passage and complete your essay. You may print out the passage, make notes, or highlight parts of the passage. Plan your essay before you start writing. Allow time to reread and proofread your essay to make any revisions or corrections. Your essay will be evaluated...  
- [Read more about Example of an Assessment Topic](/berkeley-writing-assessment/example-assessment-topic)
     
## [I enrolled in College Writing R1A and did not pass the course. May I take the BWA to satisfy the Entry Level Writing Requirement (ELWR)?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment-general-questions/i-enrolled-college-writing-r1a-and-did-not-pass)
  Once you enroll in College Writing R1A, you forgo the opportunity to take the BWA. You may only satisfy the ELWR with a grade of C or higher in College Writing R1A.  
- [Read more about I enrolled in College Writing R1A and did not pass the course. May I take the BWA to satisfy the Entry Level Writing Requirement (ELWR)?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment-general-questions/i-enrolled-college-writing-r1a-and-did-not-pass)
     
## [I have a conflict with the most recent Assessment. Are there any make-up times?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment-general-questions/i-have-conflict-most-recent-assessment-are-there)
  
Yes, the Berkeley Writing Assessment will be offered two times each year: the May administration (primarily for incoming students) and once during the fall semester. Note that you may take the Assessment only once. If you do not receive a qualifying score the first time you take the Assessment, and you have no other qualifying scores or acceptable transfer course completed prior to stating Berkeley, you should enroll in [COLWRIT R1A](https://writing.berkeley.edu/faq-page)
  
- [Read more about I have a conflict with the most recent Assessment. Are there any make-up times?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment-general-questions/i-have-conflict-most-recent-assessment-are-there)
     
## [How do I know which test scores satisfy ELWR?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment/how-do-i-know-which-test-scores-satisfy-elwr)
  
A list of accepted tests and scores is found on the [University of California Entry Level Writing Requirement(link is external)](https://admission.universityofcalifornia.edu/elwr/) page.
  
- [Read more about How do I know which test scores satisfy ELWR?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment/how-do-i-know-which-test-scores-satisfy-elwr)
     
## [Do I need to take the Assessment in order to enroll in COLWRIT R1A?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment/do-i-need-take-assessment-order-enroll-colwrit-r1a)
  
No, you may enroll directly in [COLWRIT R1A](https://writing.berkeley.edu/faq-page) without an assessment score. Many students appreciate taking the course as a way to improve their reading and writing skills in a small class environment (College Writing classes have only 14 students per section). The class is designed to set you up for success with your future writing assignments at Berkeley.
  
- [Read more about Do I need to take the Assessment in order to enroll in COLWRIT R1A?](/faq/berkeley-writing-assessment/do-i-need-take-assessment-order-enroll-colwrit-r1a)

# Example of an Assessment Topic College Writing Programs

- **Source URL**: [https://writing.berkeley.edu/berkeley-writing-assessment/example-assessment-topic](https://writing.berkeley.edu/berkeley-writing-assessment/example-assessment-topic)
- **Crawled At**: 2026-07-16T14:02:34.766Z

## Content

Below is an example of an assessment reading and question in the style you can expect for the BWA.
 
## Directions
 
- Read the passage and the essay topic that follows. Respond to the topic by writing an essay that is controlled by a central idea and is developed by discussing specific examples. 
- You will have two hours to read the passage and complete your essay. You may print out the passage, make notes, or highlight parts of the passage. Plan your essay before you start writing. Allow time to reread and proofread your essay to make any revisions or corrections. 
- Your essay will be evaluated on the basis of your ability to develop the central idea, to express yourself clearly, and to use the conventions of written English. The topic has no "correct" response.Sample Reading Passage
 
### Introductory Note
 
Daniel J. Levitin is a professor of psychology and neuroscience at McGill University, where he directs the Laboratory for Musical Perception, Cognition, and Expertise. The following passage is adapted from *This Is Your Brain on Music* by Daniel J. Levitin, copyright© 2006 by Daniel J. Levitin. Used by permission of Dutton, a division of Penguin Group (USA) Inc.
 
### Expertise Dissected
 
How do people become expert musicians? And why is it that of the millions of people who take music lessons as children, relatively few continue to play music as adults? When they find out what I do for a living, many people tell me that they love music, but that their music lessons "didn't take." I think they're being too hard on themselves. Although many people say that music lessons didn't take, cognitive neuroscientists have found otherwise in their laboratories. Even a small exposure to music lessons as a child creates neural circuits for music processing that are more efficient than those of people who lack training. Music lessons teach us to listen better, and they accelerate our ability to discern structure and form in music, making it easier for us to tell what music we like and what we don't like.
 
But what about those classes of people that we all acknowledge are true musical experts--the Alfred Brendels, Sarah Changs, Wynton Marsalises, and Tori Amoses? How did they get what most of us don't have, an extraordinary facility to play and perform?
 
The scientific study of expertise has been a major topic within cognitive science for the past thirty years, and musical expertise has tended to be studied within the context of general expertise. In almost all cases, musical expertise has been defined as technical achievement--mastery of an instrument or of compositional skills. The late Michael Howe, and his collaborators Jane Davidson and John Sloboda, launched an international debate when they asked whether the popular notion of "talent" is scientifically defensible. They assumed the following alternatives: either high levels of musical achievement are based on innate brain structures (what people refer to as talent) or they are simply the result of training and practice. They define talent as something (1) that originates in genetic structures and (2) that is identifiable at an early stage by trained people who can recognize it even before exceptional levels of performance have been acquired.
 
It is evident that some children acquire skills more rapidly than others: the ages of onset for walking, talking, and toilet training vary widely from one child to another, even within the same household. There may be genetic factors at work, but it is difficult to separate genetic factors from factors with a presumably environmental component, such as motivation, personality, and family dynamics. Similar factors can influence musical development and can mask the contributions of genetics to musical ability. Brain studies, so far, haven't been of much use in sorting out the issue because it has been difficult to separate cause from effect. For example, studies of violin players by Thomas Elbert have shown that the region of the brain responsible for moving the left hand--the hand that requires the most precision in violin playing--increases in size as a result of practice. We do not know yet if the propensity for increase preexists in the genetics of some people and not others.
 
The strongest evidence for the talent position is that some people simply acquire musical skills more rapidly than others. The evidence against the talent position--or, rather, in favor of the view that practice makes perfect--comes from research on how much training the experts or high achievement people actually do. Like experts in mathematics, chess, or sports, experts in music require lengthy periods of instruction and practice the most, sometimes twice as much as those who weren't judged as good.
 
In one study, students were secretly divided into two groups (not revealed to the students so as not to bias them) based on teachers' perceptions of their talent. Several years later, the students who achieved the highest performance ratings were those who had practiced the most, irrespective of which "talent" group they had been assigned to previously. This suggests that practice is the cause of achievement, not merely something correlated with it. It further suggests that talent is a label that we're using in a circular fashion: when we say that someone is talented, we think we mean that they have some innate predisposition to excel, but in the end, we only apply the term retrospectively, after they have made significant achievements.
 
Anders Ericsson at Florida State University and his colleagues approach the topic of musical expertise as a general problem in cognitive psychology involving how humans become experts in general. In other words, he takes as a starting assumption that there are certain issues involved in becoming an expert at anything, that we can learn about musical expertise by studying expert writers, chess players, athletes, artists, mathematicians, in addition to musicians. The emerging picture from studies of high achievers in many fields is that ten thousand hours of practice are required to achieve the level of mastery associated with being a world-class expert-in anything. In study after study--of composers, basketball players, fiction writers, ice skaters, concert pianists, chess players, master criminals, and what have you--this number comes up again and again. Ten thousand hours is equivalent to roughly three hours a day, or twenty hours a week, of practice over ten years. Of course, this doesn't address why some people don't seem to get anywhere when they practice, and why some people get more out of their practice sessions than others. But no one has yet found a case in which true world-class expertise was accomplished in less time. It seems that it takes the brain this long to assimilate all that it needs to know to achieve true mastery.
 
[Copyright© 2014 by the University of California. All rights reserved. Produced for the University of California.]
 
### Essay Topic
 
According to Levitin, what roles do talent and practice play in enabling people to reach outstanding achievements in any field? What do you think of his views? Write an essay responding to these two questions. To develop your own position, be sure to discuss your own specific examples. Those examples can be drawn from anything you've read as well as from your own observation and experience.
